title: Through a glass (1 Corinthians 13:8–13)
hookLine: now we see through a glass darkly, then face to face

lines: A FACE IN A BLACK SCREEN.
cards: Turn off a phone in a dark room and look at the black screen. You can see your face, sort of: a shape, shadows where the eyes are. That's close to what a mirror gave you in Corinth.
Mirrors then were polished metal, and even a good one showed a dim, slightly wobbly face. Paul has just said that charity never falls away.
Now he explains why almost everything else will: right now, even the wisest person is looking at a reflection.

teach.b: Prophecies will end, he says. Tongues will cease. Knowledge will be destroyed.
We know in part and we prophesy in part, and when that which is perfect comes, the partial will be done away. Then two pictures.
Growing up: when I was a child, I spoke and thought like a child, and when I became a man I put away the things of a child.
And the mirror: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face. Now I know in part; but then I shall know even as I am known."
The Greek behind in a dark manner is a phrase meaning in a riddle, and that word, ainigma, is where English gets enigma. So, in Paul's picture, faith isn't blind.
It sees something real, but indirectly, the way one works out a riddle. Look at the end of the verse, too: even as I am known. Paul's hope isn't only that he'll finally understand God.
He is already fully known, and will one day know in the same way.

teach.h: FACE TO FACE: THE BEATIFIC VISION.
teach.b: The Church calls that final seeing the beatific vision; the Catechism says the saints in heaven see God face to face, as he is, and that this is the happiness of heaven.

teach.h: THE GREATEST OF THESE IS CHARITY.
teach.b: Then Paul closes the chapter: "And now there remain faith, hope, and charity, these three: but the greatest of these is charity." Why the greatest?
Thomas Aquinas gives an answer: face to face, no one needs faith in what can't be seen, or hope for what's already given. Charity is the one that doesn't end.

how: Catholics speak of the beatific vision, the sight of God face to face, as the final hope of the Christian life; the Church teaches the saints in heaven already enjoy it.

o: a puzzle with no answer at all
a riddle, seen dimly for now
a secret code only priests can read

games.q: inside the mirror — tap the pairs.
p: a dim reflection in a mirror

s: Paul says faith sees nothing at all
it sees something real, but as in a riddle, like a dim mirror.
the Greek word behind 'dark manner' gave English 'enigma'
ancient mirrors were glass like ours
they were polished metal, with a dim reflection.

games.q: you're writing to Corinth: prophecy, tongues and knowledge will all pass. faith, hope and charity remain. which do you call the greatest?
o: knowledge, because it finally becomes complete.
games.why: "the greatest of these is charity." face to face, faith and hope are fulfilled; charity goes on.

practice: Think of something you can't figure out right now: why something happened, what comes next, what God is doing, if you believe in God.
Don't try to solve it; picture it as a face in an old metal mirror, really there but blurred, and let it stay blurred while you breathe.
If you pray, hand it over with Paul's words, now I know in part; if not, let the not-knowing sit beside you without fighting it.

wordCard.voice: Enigma. The Greek word behind seeing now in a dark manner, a riddle, until the day we see God face to face. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a riddle. 'in a dark manner' in 1 Corinthians 13:12 is literally 'in a riddle'; English gets 'enigma' from it.

carryVoice: Your line: then, face to face. For now, the mirror is still dim. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face. Now I know in part; but then I shall know even as I am known.
And now there remain faith, hope, and charity, these three: but the greatest of these is charity.

sources.ref: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II q.23 a.6
